topic: Kayaking and paddleboarding: shoulders and back

slides.headline: Kayak or SUP day on the cards?
slides.sub: How to keep your shoulders and back happy out on the water.

slides.title: Power comes from your trunk
slides.body: Whether you're in a kayak or on a paddleboard, rotating through your trunk shares the work with bigger muscles. Pulling with your arms alone tires the shoulders quickly and often leaves them sore.

slides.title: Keep the paddle close
slides.body: Reaching far out to the side puts your shoulder in a weaker position. Keep strokes close to the board or boat, with your top hand around eye height rather than high overhead.

slides.title: Soft knees on the board
slides.body: On a paddleboard, stand with feet hip-width apart and knees slightly bent. Locked knees push more work into your lower back. Kneeling for a while is a handy break.

slides.title: Build up your time on the water
slides.body: Your first paddle of summer isn't the time for a three-hour trip. Start with 30 to 45 minutes, take breaks, and build up over a few outings as your shoulders adapt.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Shoulder pain that wakes you at night, weakness lifting your arm, pins and needles in the hand, or back pain spreading down a leg is worth assessing rather than paddling through.

slides.headline: Sore after your last paddle?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your shoulder and back, then build a plan to get you paddling comfortably again. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Paddled out feeling great, drove home with sore shoulders and a stiff back?

Kayaking and paddleboarding are fantastic summer exercise, but the first few outings often ask more of your shoulders and back than they're used to.

A few tweaks usually help: turn through your trunk rather than pulling with your arms, keep the paddle close to the board, soften your knees on a SUP, and build up your time on the water over several trips instead of starting with a marathon.
